Scientists once calculated the exact day humanity would end. Friday, November thirteenth, 2026. Just twelve days ago.
In 1960, physicist Heinz von Foerster and two colleagues studied two thousand years of world population.
And they noticed something scary. It wasn't just growing. It was growing faster and faster.
More people meant more parents, more ideas, more food, and even more people.
They fitted a formula to the numbers, and the curve shot straight up.
On Friday, November thirteenth, 2026, the number of people would become infinite.
Not the end of the world by asteroid. The end of the world by standing room only.
The date even fell on von Foerster's hundred and fifteenth birthday.
It was meant as a warning. And then, something changed.
In the nineteen sixties, the world's growth rate peaked, and started to fall.
Families got smaller, as more children survived and more people moved to cities.
Today there are about eight billion of us. Not infinity.
And the United Nations expects the population to peak later this century.
So doomsday came and went. And you're still here, scrolling.
